blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
blocks.content: 1. Problem Statement

blocks.text:
Picture a single public API endpoint the moment it becomes popular. Most of the traffic hitting it is completely legitimate, real users doing real things, but somewhere in that traffic there is also a misconfigured retry loop hammering the same endpoint a thousand times a second, a scraper trying to pull an entire catalog in one afternoon, and occasionally something worse, a credential stuffing attack trying thousands of password guesses as fast as the server will accept them.

A rate limiter is the piece of infrastructure that decides, for every single request, whether it gets to proceed or gets turned away, based on how many requests that same client has already made in some recent window of time. It sits close to the front door of the system, before expensive work happens, and it is one of the few pieces of infrastructure that is simultaneously a performance safeguard, a cost control, a fairness mechanism between tenants, and a security control against abuse.

So the job here is precise: build a service that can answer the question "has this client already used up its budget" in a few milliseconds, correctly, for every request flowing through a system that might be running on hundreds of stateless application servers at once. Everything else in this document, the four algorithms, the distributed coordination, the failure handling, exists to answer that one question reliably at scale.

blocks.text: 2.3 How limits vary by plan or tier
blocks.content: 2.3 How limits vary by plan or tier

blocks.text: Real products almost never ship with one flat number. A reasonable shape: each client belongs to a plan, each plan maps to a policy, and each policy defines one or more rules, a limit value, a window size, and which algorithm backs it, scoped to a particular endpoint or endpoint group. Changing a limit should be a configuration change, never a code deploy, since a limit that needs a full release cycle to adjust is a limit that will not get adjusted fast enough when it actually matters.

blocks.text: 5.1 Why per-user and per-IP together, not just one
blocks.content: 5.1 Why per-user and per-IP together, not just one

blocks.text: It is tempting to pick a single dimension and move on, but each one alone has an obvious hole. Per user alone does nothing for anonymous, unauthenticated traffic, which is exactly where scraping and credential stuffing tend to live. Per IP alone breaks down the moment real users sit behind a shared corporate network address translation gateway or a mobile carrier network address translation pool, where thousands of legitimate users can appear to share one address. Layering both, plus a stricter per endpoint budget for anything expensive, covers the gaps each one leaves behind on its own.

blocks.text: 6.2 How much memory does the counter store need
blocks.content: 6.2 How much memory does the counter store need

blocks.text: Assume roughly 2 million distinct active rate limit keys during a busy hour, a mix of users, IP addresses, and API keys that have made at least one request recently. A fixed window counter is cheap: one small integer plus an expiry per key, call it about 60 bytes once Redis internal overhead is included. Two million keys times 60 bytes comes out to about 114 megabytes, trivially small for a modern Redis cluster.

A fixed window counter is cheap: one small integer plus an expiry per key, call it about 60 bytes once Redis internal overhead is included. blocks.text: Now compare that to a sliding window log, which keeps one entry per request inside the window rather than a single integer. If the average active key has around 20 requests sitting in its window, and each sorted set member costs roughly 90 bytes of overhead in Redis, that is 2,000,000 times 20 times 90, which comes out to about 3.4 gigabytes, nearly 30 times heavier than the fixed window approach for the exact same traffic. Push every key to the worst case, a full 100 entries each, and that climbs to roughly 16.8 gigabytes for this one limiting dimension alone. That gap is the real, concrete cost behind the memory tradeoff explored in Section 8 and Section 24.

blocks.text: 7.2 Why a single in-process counter breaks
blocks.content: 7.2 Why a single in-process counter breaks
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229164416-98270374.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229164416-98270374.png
blocks.alt: Three gateway instances each keeping their own local counter of 40 requests add up to a real total of 120, blowing past a limit of 100 without any single instance ever knowing it

blocks.text: The most natural first instinct, keep a counter in memory inside each gateway process, works perfectly on a single server and falls apart the moment there is more than one. With three gateway instances behind a load balancer, a client sending 120 requests might get spread roughly evenly, 40 requests to each instance. Every single instance sees only 40 requests and cheerfully reports "well under the limit of 100," while the client has, in reality, made 120. This is not a rare edge case, it is the default outcome of horizontal scaling, and it is the entire reason this document exists.

blocks.content: 7.3 The distributed rate limiting picture

blocks.alt: Three different gateway instances all issue the same atomic check-and-increment call against the same Redis key, and Redis single threaded execution model guarantees they get serialized correctly

blocks.text: The fix is to stop trying to make each instance smart, and instead make them all agree by asking the same question of the same shared store. Every gateway instance, no matter which one a given request happens to land on, resolves the same key for the same client and issues the same atomic check-and-increment call against the same Redis cluster. Redis becomes the one place where truth about "how many requests has this client made" actually lives.

blocks.text: 8.3 Fixed Window Counter
blocks.content: 8.3 Fixed Window Counter
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229171863-664145863.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229171863-664145863.png
blocks.alt: Two adjacent one minute windows, each individually satisfying a limit of 100, but a burst landing right at the boundary between them lets 200 requests through in about two real seconds

blocks.text: The simplest possible approach: divide time into fixed, non overlapping windows, say one minute each, aligned to the clock, and keep a single counter per key per window. Every request increments the counter for whichever window contains the current time, and gets rejected once that counter exceeds the limit. When the clock rolls into a new window, the counter simply resets to zero.

Every request increments the counter for whichever window contains the current time, and gets rejected once that counter exceeds the limit. blocks.text: The problem is entirely at the edges. Suppose the limit is 100 requests per minute, and a client sends 100 requests in the last second of window one, at 10:00:59, all allowed since the window one counter reaches exactly 100. The clock rolls over to 10:01:00, window two opens with a fresh counter at zero, and the same client immediately sends another 100 requests in the first second of window two, all allowed again, since window two independently has not touched its own limit yet. The result: 200 requests accepted within roughly two real seconds, double the intended rate, simply because the two bursts happened to straddle a window boundary. Both individual windows technically respected the rule, and the client still got twice its budget.

blocks.text: 8.4 Sliding Window Log
blocks.content: 8.4 Sliding Window Log
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229173505-149727427.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229173505-149727427.png
blocks.alt: A rolling 60 second window keeps every timestamp that falls inside it and discards anything older, giving an exact count with no boundary artifact at all

blocks.text: This fixes the boundary problem directly by refusing to use fixed, clock aligned windows at all. Instead, every request timestamp gets recorded, and on each new request, anything older than the window size gets discarded, and whatever remains is the exact count of requests in the trailing window, right now, no matter where the clock happens to sit. In Redis terms this is naturally a sorted set, one member per request, scored by its timestamp.

blocks.text: The accuracy is genuinely perfect, there is no boundary artifact of any kind, because there is no boundary. The cost is memory: a fixed window needs one integer per key, while a sliding log needs one entry per request inside the window. Section 6.2 already worked the arithmetic, at a limit of 100 requests per minute with 2 million active keys, this can run anywhere from about 3.4 gigabytes in the typical case to nearly 17 gigabytes in the worst case, versus about 114 megabytes for a fixed window covering the identical traffic. That gap is the whole tradeoff in one number.

blocks.text: Work through the same boundary case from Section 8.3 with this approach. The previous window closed with 100 requests. It is now 10:01:15, fifteen seconds, or 25 percent, into the new window, so the previous window still contributes 75 percent of its weight. The current window has already logged 10 new requests. The estimate becomes 10 plus 100 times 0.75, which is 85, comfortably communicating that this client is still close to its limit rather than pretending, the way a naive fixed window would, that a fresh 100 request budget just opened up. blocks.alt: Tokens refill into a bucket at a steady rate up to its capacity, each request consumes one token, and a request only gets rejected once the bucket is empty

blocks.text: Picture a bucket that holds up to a fixed number of tokens, say 100, and refills at a steady rate, say 1.67 tokens per second, which works out to 100 per minute over time. blocks.alt: Bursty arrivals get held in a fixed size queue and drained to the backend at a strict constant rate, so the backend itself never sees anything faster than that steady leak rate

blocks.text: Leaky bucket looks similar on paper but solves a different problem. Requests arrive into a fixed size queue, and get processed, or leaked, out the other end at a strict, constant rate, regardless of how bursty the arrivals were. Take 150 requests arriving in a single burst against a queue capacity of 100 and a leak rate of 1.67 per second: the first 100 get queued, the remaining 50 are dropped immediately because the queue is already full, and the accepted 100 then trickle out to the backend one by one at that fixed 1.67 per second rate.

blocks.alt: Two gateway instances both read a count of 99, both independently decide 99 is under the limit of 100, and both write back, letting one request through that should have been rejected

blocks.text: Walk through the exact failure. The limit is 100. Two different gateway instances, A and B, each receive one request for the same user at almost the same instant. Both call GET on the same Redis key and both see the current count as 99. Both, independently, compute 99 plus 1 is 100, which is not over the limit of 100, so both decide to allow. Both then write the counter to 100. The end result: two requests were allowed on top of an already-at-99 count, when only one should have been, and the stored value of 100 does not even reveal that anything went wrong, since 100 is exactly at the limit. This is a textbook check then act race condition, and it gets worse, not better, as concurrency increases.

blocks.text: The fix is to never let application code see an intermediate state at all. A small Lua script, loaded once into Redis and invoked with EVALSHA, performs the read, the comparison, and the increment as one indivisible unit. Redis executes Lua scripts on a single thread, which means for the duration of that script, nothing else touches the key. The second gateway instance in the same scenario now genuinely sees the count that the first instance already wrote, because there is no gap in time where it could observe stale data, and it correctly gets rejected.

blocks.text: None of these components exist in isolation, and the boundaries between them are deliberate. blocks.text: 11.1 SQL for policy, Redis for counters
blocks.content: 11.1 SQL for policy, Redis for counters

blocks.text: This system deliberately splits across two very different storage technologies rather than forcing everything into one. Policy data is small, relational in shape, changes rarely, and benefits from real transactions when an admin edits several rules together, which is exactly what a conventional SQL database is good at. Counters are the opposite in every dimension: enormous in request volume, trivial in size per record, short lived, and need atomic, sub-millisecond operations, which is exactly what an in-memory key-value store like Redis is built for. Using one database for both would mean compromising badly on at least one side.

blocks.alt: Each of the four algorithms maps naturally onto a different Redis data structure: a plain string for fixed window, a sorted set for sliding log, and a hash for token bucket

blocks.text: A fixed window counter is a single Redis STRING holding an integer, with EXPIRE set on the very first request of a window so the key vanishes on its own once the window naturally ends. A sliding window log is a ZSET, one member per request, scored by timestamp, trimmed on every read by removing anything older than the window. A token bucket is a HASH holding two fields, the current token count and the timestamp of the last refill, recomputed on every check. Choosing the right structure per algorithm is not a style preference, it directly determines the memory arithmetic worked out in Section 6.2.

blocks.text: There is no LRU eviction policy at play here the way there would be for a traditional cache, since every counter key is given an explicit TTL matching its own window size the moment it is created. blocks.alt: When the Redis cluster becomes unreachable, the system defaults to failing open, allowing traffic through, except on a short list of endpoints explicitly marked sensitive enough to fail closed instead

blocks.text: This is the single most consequential reliability decision in the whole design, and it deserves to be stated plainly: what should happen to every single request if the counter store itself is unreachable? There are exactly two honest answers. Fail open means letting requests through with no rate limiting at all until the store recovers, protecting overall availability at the cost of temporarily losing the protection the limiter exists to provide. Fail closed means rejecting every request until the store recovers, protecting the backend at the cost of taking down the entire API over what might just be a rate limiter blip.

blocks.title: Why most teams default to fail open
blocks.text: A rate limiter is a protective layer, not the primary service. Failing closed turns a localized Redis problem into a full platform outage, which is almost always a worse outcome than a brief window of reduced protection. The default in this design is fail open, with an explicit, narrow exception: endpoints doing something genuinely dangerous without any limit at all, like a login attempt counter guarding against brute force attacks, are configured to fail closed instead, since briefly having zero protection there is a real security risk, not just an inconvenience.

import threading

# The actual Lua script a production system loads into Redis and invokes with
# EVALSHA. Redis executes every script on a single thread, which is what makes
# the read, compare, and increment atomic across every calling instance.
CHECK_AND_INCREMENT_SCRIPT = """
local current = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
if current + 1 > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
  return 0
else
  redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
  if current == 0 then
    redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
  end
  return 1
end
"""


class RedisAtomicRateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, limit):
        self.limit = limit
        # a tiny in-process stand-in for a real Redis client
        self._simulated_store = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def check_and_increment(self, key):
        # the lock below mirrors the atomicity a real EVALSHA call gets from Redis itself
        with self._lock:
            current = self._simulated_store.get(key, 0)
            if current + 1 > self.limit:
                return False
            self._simulated_store[key] = current + 1
            return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    limiter = RedisAtomicRateLimiter(3)
    for i in range(5):
        print(f"gateway node request {i} allowed={limiter.check_and_increment('user:42')}")
